papers.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Risk of Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Epidemiologic studies suggest that type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC). However, prior meta-analyses have relied heavily on studies published more than a decade ago and have often combined distinct epidemiologic effect measures. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies published from January 2012 through January 2026 evaluating the association between T2DM and incident CRC. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and Scopus were searched, and eligible studies reporting associations between T2DM and CRC were included. Effect estimates were synthesized separately using random-effects models to calculate pooled estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Sex-specific and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were also conducted. Fourteen studies were included, comprising nine cohort and five case-control studies; six reported odds ratios (ORs), seven reported hazard ratios (HRs), and one reported a standardized incidence ratio (SIR). T2DM was associated with higher odds of incident CRC (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.13-1.46) and a higher hazard of incident CRC (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.23-1.31). The study reporting an SIR also showed higher CRC incidence among individuals with T2DM (SIR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.39-1.45). Sex-specific analyses generally showed positive associations in both females and males, and sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the pooled findings. Overall, T2DM was associated with an increased risk of incident CRC, with a consistent direction of association across distinct epidemiologic effect measures. These findings provide updated evidence supporting consideration of T2DM as a marker of increased CRC risk and may inform CRC prevention strategies among individuals with T2DM.

papers.title: Prevalence of Self-Reported Auditory Dysfunction Among Call Center Employees and Its Association with Shift Work Across Various Call Centers in Cairo, Egypt, March 2026
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The rapid, unregulated expansion of the call center industry in developing countries has increased occupational health risks for young adults, particularly with regard to auditory health. Prolonged exposure to acoustic trauma, long working hours, and the high intensity nature of call center work can negatively affect young adults at the start of their working lives and may contribute to permanent noise induced hearing loss (NIHL). This damage is often irreversible but preventable if identified at an early stage. This study aims to evaluate the burden of auditory impairment among call center employees in Egypt and to propose evidence based mitigation strategies. Methods A pilot cross sectional study was conducted among employees of various medical call centers over approximately three months (January to March 2026). Participants were recruited through voluntary (self selected) sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire on work history, and statistical analysis was performed to examine associations with work duration and intensity. Three semi structured, open ended interviews were conducted in March 2026 to explore the symptoms in greater depth. Results Forty six call center employees completed the questionnaire. The most frequently reported symptoms were mishearing words (82.6%), difficulty understanding speech in background noise (80.4%), needing others to repeat themselves (78.3%), and sensitivity to loud sounds (78.3%); 60.9% reported tinnitus. Higher auditory symptom severity was associated with a history of acoustic shock (Mann Whitney U = 344.0, p = .004) and with greater cognitive symptom burden (Spearman's {rho} = .416, p = .004), but not significantly with shift type (p = .177), years of work (p = .885), or daily and weekly working hours. Qualitative interviews described auditory strain that builds through the shift, disrupted sleep, informal coping, and the absence of employer guidance or symptom reporting pathways. Conclusion and Recommendations Self reported auditory symptoms were common in this preliminary sample of call center employees and were associated with acoustic shock exposure and cognitive symptom burden, but not significantly with shift pattern or length of service. Because the study was cross sectional, relied on self reports, and used a small volunteer sample (pilot study), the findings cannot establish causation or true prevalence. Recommended measures include acoustic shock limiters with incident reporting, audiometric screening that prioritizes at risk employees, safe volume education with regular breaks, and educational programs on auditory hazards and early warning signs to prevent actual auditory damage. Larger multi site studies with audiometric confirmation are also needed. Keywords: noise induced hearing loss; call center employees; occupational health; auditory dysfunction; tinnitus; acoustic shock; shift work; Egypt

papers.title: Pneumococcal nasopharyngeal carriage in children 2-60 months of age in Novi Sad (Serbia), October 2022-September 2026
papers.abstract: Background: Streptococcus pneumoniae nasopharyngeal carriage in young children is an important source of transmission and may precede pneumococcal disease. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines can alter circulating serotypes. Continued surveillance is needed to monitor serotype replacement, vaccine serotype coverage, and antimicrobial resistance. Methods: A prospective surveillance study was conducted in outpatient pediatric practices from October 2022 to September 2026 among children aged 2-60 months in Novi Sad, Serbia. Healthy children attending preventive visits and children with acute respiratory tract infections were enrolled. Nasopharyngeal specimens were collected and cultured for S. pneumoniae. Participant-level analyses used the first eligible specimen per child, while isolate-level analyses included all recovered isolates. Serotyping and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were performed. Theoretical vaccine serotype coverage was estimated for licensed and selected investigational pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, with 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine evaluated separately. Results: Among 3,373 included children, 911 were pneumococcal carriers, giving an overall carriage prevalence of 27.0%. Carriage was higher among children with acute respiratory tract infection than among healthy children and was also associated with daycare attendance, chronic medical conditions, age, season, and surveillance year. In total, 1,312 pneumococcal isolates were recovered, of which 87.9% were typeable. The most frequent serotypes included 11A, 10A, 15A, 15B, 23A, 23B, 19A, and 6B. Theoretical serotype coverage was 8.2% for PCV10, 17.5% for PCV13, 20.0% for PCV15, and 47.3% for PCV20. More than half of typeable isolates were non-PCV20 serotypes. Resistance was most frequent to erythromycin, clindamycin, and tetracycline, while multidrug resistance was observed in 18.1% of isolates. Penicillin G non-susceptibility was uncommon. Conclusion: Pneumococcal carriage in children aged 2-60 months in Novi Sad was associated with age, clinical presentation, season, and surveillance year and involved diverse serotypes. Continued carriage surveillance, linked with invasive-disease and antibiotic-use data, would help determine whether the observed serotype and resistance patterns persist.

papers.title: Socioeconomic position, socioenvironmental conditions, and subjective cognitive decline among midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults in California
papers.abstract: Objectives: To examine which measure of socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions has the strongest relationship with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) among midlife and older lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, and other sexual and gender minority (LGBTQIA+) adults. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 3869 LGBTQIA+ adults aged 50 years or older participating in a community-engaged survey in California. Using logistic regression, we examined overall associations between each indicator of socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions and SCD. We used a dominance analysis to assess the relative importance of each indicator based on the proportion of variance in SCD it explained. Results: Overall, 14.7% of the sample reported SCD. Midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults in a lower socioeconomic position (i.e., lower education, unemployment, lower household income, fewer assets, financial insecurity, food insecurity, and unstable housing) had higher odds of SCD than those in a higher position, with significant odds ratios (OR) ranging from 1.44 to 1.93. In contrast, perceiving one's community as safe for LGBTQIA+ people was associated with lower odds of SCD (OR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.48, 0.76). Dominance analysis indicated that household assets was the most important factor, explaining 2.8% of the variance in SCD (95% CI 2.2%, 3.6%), followed by household income (1.9%; 95% CI 1.2%, 2.7%) and perceived community safety (1.6%; 95% CI 1.1%, 2.3%). Discussion: Supporting the cognitive health of LGBTQIA+ people may require attention to both financial security across the life course and the broader social environments.

papers.title: Epidemiology of zero-dose among children aged 12-35 months in Ethiopia: Burden, correlates and spatial patterns; Evidence from a 2025 national survey
papers.abstract: Background: Children who have not received the first dose of a diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-containing vaccine are classified as zero-dose. Understanding how many children remain without this dose beyond infancy, the correlates, and their geographic distribution can inform routine and catch-up vaccination services in Ethiopia. This study aimed to estimate the burden of zero-dose, identify its correlates, and map its spatial distribution among children aged 12-35 months in Ethiopia. Methods: We analyzed data from 2,097 children aged 12-35 months in the Pathways for Ethiopia survey, a recent national population-based cross-sectional household survey conducted from August to November 2025. The burden estimates and regression analyses accounted for sampling weights, stratification, and clustering. Adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) were obtained through marginal standardization of survey-weighted logistic regression models. Spatial autocorrelation, hotspot, and spatial-scan analyses assessed geographic clustering. Ordinary kriging predicted prevalence at unsampled locations. Results: The weighted prevalence of zero-dose status was 20.6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 15.9-26.3), with regional point estimates ranging from 0.8% in Addis Ababa to 35.9% in Somali. Its burden was 20.4% among children aged 12-23 months and 20.8% among those aged 24-35 months. Higher burden was associated with no antenatal care compared with four or more visits (aPR: 2.39; 95% CI: 1.61-3.53), unimproved compared with improved drinking-water sources (aPR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.18-1.97), and caregivers rating vaccination as less than very important compared with very important (aPR: 2.68; 95% CI: 2.03-3.54). Zero-dose prevalence showed significant spatial clustering (Morans I = 0.229; p = 0.0001). Hotspots occurred among sampled communities in Somali, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, Afar, and South Ethiopia. Predicted prevalence was highest across parts of eastern and south-central Ethiopia. Conclusion: Approximately one in five children aged 12-35 months had not received the first pentavalent dose. High zero-dose prevalence clustered among sampled communities in eastern and south-central Ethiopia. Moreover, antenatal care and drinking water source were independent factors. Immunization programs should prioritize these communities for identifying and vaccinating missed children, including those aged 24-35 months.

papers.title: Associations between different intensities of leisure-time physical activity and subsequent psychotropic medication use among young and early midlife adults: a register-linked follow-up study
papers.abstract: Introduction Previous studies have not examined associations between physical activity intensity and subsequent psychotropic medication use. We examined associations between different leisure-time physical activity (LTPA) intensities and subsequent psychotropic medication purchases. Methods We used Helsinki Health Study questionnaire data collected in 2017 from 19-39-year-old employees of the City of Helsinki, linked to register data on psychotropic medication purchases from 2014 to 2022 (82.5% consented to the register linkage). The analytical sample included 4,160 participants (80.4% women, representing the target population). Weekly hours of light (LPA), moderate (MPA) and vigorous (VPA) LTPA were examined separately. Cox proportional hazards regression with restricted cubic splines was used to examine nonlinear associations with the first psychotropic medication purchase during follow-up, adjusting for prior medication and sociodemographic and health-related covariates. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Results During the follow-up, 28.1% of participants had at least one psychotropic medication purchase. After adjustment for age and gender, VPA was associated with psychotropic medication purchases (overall p<0.001; nonlinearity p<0.001), whereas MPA and LPA were not. Further adjustments and stratification by prior psychotropic medication purchase status attenuated the VPA association (overall p=0.0041). In this model, for 5 versus 0 hours/week of VPA, the HR was 0.79 (95% CI 0.68-0.91), corresponding to approximately 23 fewer first-purchase events per 1,000 participants over three years. Conclusions Higher-intensity LTPA appeared more strongly associated with a lower hazard of psychotropic medication purchases, although only the VPA association saw clear support.

papers.title: Beyond the 24-Hour Rhythm: Functional Principal Components of Daily Activity Residuals and Mortality in NHANES
papers.abstract: begin{abstract} noindenttextbf{Background.} Accelerometer-derived 24-hour activity profiles are usually summarised by cosinor rhythm parameters or by functional principal component analysis (FPCA). Applied to the raw profiles, however, the leading functional components largely re-express what the cosinor already captures: activity level, rhythm strength and timing. Whether the shape of the day carries health information beyond these parameters is unclear. noindenttextbf{Methods.} We analysed adults with seven valid days of accelerometry from two National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohorts: hip activity counts (2003--2006; $n = 2{,}615$) and wrist Monitor-Independent Movement Summary units (2011--2014; $n = 3{,}208$). Minute-level activity was transformed with the inverse hyperbolic sine, and a single 24-hour cosinor curve was fitted across each participant's seven days. Each participant's average residual curve, which contains no 24-hour component, was decomposed by FPCA and, to separate stable between-person patterns from day-to-day variation, by multilevel FPCA. In exploratory analyses, we related the three leading components to all-cause mortality and, secondarily, to cardiovascular and cancer mortality. We used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, income and the cosinor parameters, with the hip cohort for discovery and the wrist cohort for replication. noindenttextbf{Results.} The three leading residual components explained 44% (hip) and 51% (wrist) of residual variance and consisted mainly of 12-hour and 8-hour patterns. The second component (FPC2) contrasts an early-starting, flat day with a day of distinct mid-morning and evening peaks. Its shape was nearly identical in the two cohorts (similarity 0.96), and multilevel FPCA recovered it as a stable between-person pattern. In unweighted models, FPC2 was the only component associated with all-cause mortality in the discovery cohort (hazard ratio per SD 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.29; Benjamini--Hochberg $q = 0.008$), and the association replicated in the wrist cohort (1.18, 1.03 to 1.35; $p = 0.017$). With survey weights that also accounted for selection into the analytic sample, the association was concentrated in cardiovascular deaths (hip 1.53, 1.12 to 2.09, $p = 0.007$; wrist 1.38, 1.10 to 1.72, $p = 0.005$). This association persisted after further adjustment for lifestyle factors and traditional activity metrics. FPC2 was not associated with cancer mortality. Scores of the leading components did not form distinct clusters (average silhouette width $leq 0.23$), but FPC2 was selected as a continuous predictor of cardiovascular mortality in both cohorts by forward selection on 10-fold cross-validated, survey-weighted AUC. noindenttextbf{Conclusions.} The within-day structure of activity that a 24-hour cosinor cannot represent varies continuously between people. One replicated aspect of it, the loss of a two-peak daily pattern, was associated with mortality beyond rhythm strength and timing, most clearly cardiovascular mortality. The shape of daily activity therefore carries prognostic information beyond standard rhythm summaries. It can support mortality risk prediction that needs only a few personal details, and may help identify individuals at elevated risk and tailor interventions to their daily activity patterns. medskip noindenttextbf{Keywords:} functional principal component analysis, cosinor, rest-activity rhythm, mortality, accelerometry end{abstract}

papers.title: Resting Heart Rate for Global Health Surveillance: Descriptive Epidemiology of 566,986 Participants from the WHO STEP Surveys and the South Asia Biobank
papers.abstract: Objective: To describe global patterns of resting heart rate (RHR) in population subgroups and over time. Methods: Observational data from WHO STEP surveys (n=363,462 participants from 76 countries, 2002-2020) and the South Asia Biobank (SAB, n=203,524 participants from four South Asian countries, 2018-2023). RHR was measured in triplicate while seated using a blood pressure cuff. Height and weight were measured using anthropometric techniques. Physical activity was self-reported and accelerometry-measured (SAB subsample, n=22,183). We describe RHR distributions by geographical region, temporality, sex, age, BMI, and physical activity. Utility of RHR to explain accelerometer-based physical activity was examined by regression. Results: Country-level median RHR ranged 65-80 bpm, higher in women than men. Age-related RHR patterns diverged markedly by sex; men showing a curvilinear association with higher RHR in midlife, and women showing a consistent decline with age across most regions. Compared to normal-weight, obese participants had higher RHR [WHO: (men: +4.4 bpm, women: +0.9 bpm), SAB: (men: +3.1 bpm, women: +1.0 bpm)]. Participants meeting physical activity recommendations had lower RHR [WHO: (men: -1.6 bpm, women: -0.9 bpm), SAB: (men: -2.1 bpm, women: -0.5 bpm)] compared to insufficiently active. In SAB (field-work spanning whole-calendar year), seasonal variations were present (0.6-0.9 bpm higher RHR in June-August compared to September-November), most pronounced further from the equator. In 21 WHO countries with repeat survey data, RHR was stable over time in women but declined in men (-0.4 bpm/year). Self-reported activity explained 2-14% (women: 2-3%, men: 10-14%) of the variance in device-measured physical activity, and RHR added 1-3% incrementally. Conclusions: RHR varies globally, exhibits different age-related patterns by sex, and is higher in population subgroups with greater non-communicable disease burden. RHR is easy to measure and may have utility for global health surveillance.

papers.title: El Nino Southern Oscillation shapes cholera in Africa
papers.abstract: Cholera is considered a paradigm for climate-sensitive diseases, yet its relation with El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, remains poorly quantified in Africa where most cholera deaths occur. Using 15 years of surveillance data across 30 African countries and novel statistical and simulation frameworks, we identify five geographically coherent ENSO-cholera teleconnection groups, each characterized by distinct directions, strengths and timing of effects on outbreak occurrence, duration and incidence. For the unfolding major El Nino of 2026-27, we project two- to five-fold greater cholera burden in Eastern and Horn of Africa than under ENSO-neutral conditions. These findings identify immediate priorities for anticipatory action and establish a dynamic framework for attributing burden for outbreak-prone diseases to climate variability.

papers.title: Factors associated with congenital syphilis among women with gestational syphilis in a public health network in Bogota, Colombia, 2017-2024: A case-control study
papers.abstract: Background Congenital syphilis remains a preventable cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, and its incidence in Colombia remains well above the elimination target. We aimed to identify maternal and prenatal care factors associated with congenital syphilis among women with gestational syphilis attended in a public health network serving socially vulnerable populations in Bogota, Colombia. Methods We conducted a retrospective case-control study using surveillance and clinical records from the Subred Integrada de Servicios de Salud Sur E.S.E. for pregnancies ending between 2017 and 2024. Cases were neonates with congenital syphilis according to national surveillance criteria; controls were neonates without congenital syphilis born to mothers with gestational syphilis in the same network. Factors associated with congenital syphilis were identified using multivariable logistic regression with backward elimination. Results We included 743 mother-infant pairs (285 cases and 458 controls). Maternal diagnosis after 28 weeks of gestation (adjusted odds ratio 17.75; 95% confidence interval 11.81-26.69), absence of prenatal care compared with eight or more visits (12.74; 5.03-32.25) and reinfection during pregnancy (3.02; 1.73-5.29) were independently associated with congenital syphilis, whereas a documented history of syphilis was associated with lower odds (0.45; 0.25-0.82). The model showed high discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.860). Migrant status was associated with congenital syphilis in the crude analysis but not after adjustment. Conclusions Congenital syphilis in this setting was associated mainly with late maternal diagnosis and absent prenatal care, conditions that preclude timely benzathine penicillin treatment. Strengthening early prenatal screening, continuity of care and partner management may reduce vertical transmission in socially vulnerable urban populations.

papers.title: Discrete dynamic survival analysis of epidemic case line lists
papers.abstract: Case line lists, which record dates of onset, recovery, and hospitalisation, are among the most granular data in infectious disease epidemiology and can provide insights into transmission dynamics. Dynamic survival analysis (DSA) fits a deterministic, differential-equation-based model to line lists to estimate parameters such as infectivity and the infectious period. Infectious periods are usually not exponential, and incorporating this into mechanistic models for line-list data often requires partial differential equation (PDE) schemes that can be difficult to implement and must be customised for each model, which may limit their use. Here, we propose Discrete Dynamic Survival Analysis (DDSA), a discrete-time DSA for case line lists based on difference equations. It matches calendar-day data directly without interpolation, and its log-likelihood is differentiable via forward-mode automatic differentiation, enabling off-the-shelf gradient-based samplers without model-specific numerical infrastructure. Non-exponential infectious periods are accommodated through a boxcar model or a discrete analogue of the "device of stages". We apply the DDSA method to three historical outbreaks of influenza A(H1N1), Ebola, and measles. DDSA estimates of transmission parameters were close to published analyses where these were available, an agreement that partly reflects shared modelling choices, and the method handles incomplete line lists with missing onset or recovery dates. Synthetic experiments show that recovery intervals identify the infectious period, while infection times and final size constrain R0 when the population at risk is known. Discrete DSA provides a simple, extensible framework for simulation and inference of infectious disease dynamics.

papers.title: Influenza Vaccination and Disease Severity Among Older Adults Hospitalized with Influenza in France: A Nationwide Cohort Study, 2016-2024
papers.abstract: Objective Seasonal influenza remains a major cause of severe morbidity and mortality among older adults, despite vaccine availability. We assessed whether influenza vaccination was associated with reduced disease severity among adults aged 65 years or more hospitalized with influenza in France. Methods and Analysis We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the French National Health Data System (SNDS). Adults aged 65 years or more hospitalized with confirmed influenza (ICD-10 codes: J09 or J10) between October 2016 and December 2024 were included, excluding 2020-2021. Vaccination status was identified from reimbursed community pharmacy dispensing records. Entropy balancing was used to balance sociodemographic characteristics, chronic conditions pneumococcal vaccination, and COVID-19 vaccination. Weighted regression models estimated adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) for invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), intensive care unit (ICU) admission, in-hospital death, and a composite severe outcome. Multistate survival models assessed transitions specific hazard ratios (HR) between hospitalization, ICU, discharge, and in-hospital death. Results Among 132,443 influenza-associated hospitalizations, 72,852 (55%) occurred among vaccinated patients and 59,591 (45%) among unvaccinated patients. Vaccinated patients were older (mean age, 82.3 vs 79.3 years). IMV occurred in 2128 vaccinated (2.9%) and 2544 unvaccinated (4.3%) hospitalizations (aRR, 0.88; 95%CI: 0.83 to 0.93). In-hospital death occurred in 6300 (8.6%) and 4952 (8.3%), respectively (aRR, 0.90; 95%CI: 0.87 to 0.93). Vaccination was also associated with a lower risk of the composite outcome (aRR, 0.96; 95%CI: 0.94 to 0.98), but not ICU admission (aRR, 0.99; 95%CI: 0.96 to 1.01). Among patients admitted to ICU, vaccination was associated with a lower hazard of death (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.85; 95%CI: 0.78 to 0.92) and a 2-day reduction in the median time to discharge. Conclusion In this nationwide cohort study, influenza vaccination was associated with lower risks of IMV and in-hospital death among older adults hospitalized with influenza. These findings are consistent with possible attenuation of disease severity and support efforts to improve influenza vaccination among older adults.

papers.title: Associations of drinking water per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances with cause-specific mortality in men with prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Background: Over 3.5 million US men are living with prostate cancer (PCa). Certain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are carcinogenic and impair cardiometabolic health. Due to comorbidities and treatment, men with PCa may be uniquely susceptible to PFAS. Objectives: To develop and validate a model for drinking water perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), and study associations of each PFAS with all-cause, PCa, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in PCa survivors. Methods: We conducted a cohort study of 51,289 men with PCa diagnosed from 2006 to 2017 and followed through 2024 from the New Jersey (NJ) cancer registry. PFAS monitoring data (n=26,161 results) were obtained from NJ government evaluations and Community Water Systems (CWS) compliance reports and were used to estimate PFAS concentrations using a two-phase XGBoost model with 67 predictors of PFAS contamination across 566 CWS. PFAS predictions between 2006-2024 were linked to participant address histories. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated from Cox models with sociodemographic, clinical and time-varying neighborhood covariates. Results: There were 19,749 deaths, including 3,778 PCa deaths, and 4,972 CVD deaths over 466,843 person-years. Higher PFOA exposure was associated with all-cause mortality in certain quintiles (aHRQ2vsQ1: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.07-1.12; aHRQ3vsQ1: 1.06, 95% CI: 1.01-1.11) and with CVD mortality (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.12, 95% CI: 1.01-1.24). Higher PFNA exposure was suggestively associated with all-cause mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.22, 95% CI: 0.98-1.50) and PCa mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.42, 95% CI: 0.96-2.10). Associations were strengthened when applying five-year lags. For example, higher PFOA (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.06-1.25), PFOS (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.07-1.25) and PFNA (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.57, 95% CI: 1.06-2.31) were associated with higher all-cause mortality. Discussion: Exposure to CWS-level PFAS was associated with higher mortality in PCa survivors. Replication is needed to confirm findings.

papers.title: Sex-Specific Incidence of Hemorrhagic Stroke in Japan: An Integrated Population-Based Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundIntracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) have contrasting epidemiological characteristics, including sex-specific incidence. However, their overall contribution to sex differences in hemorrhagic stroke remains unclear because they are generally evaluated separately. We examined the sex-specific epidemiology of hemorrhagic stroke by integrating ICH and SAH. MethodsWe analyzed first-ever ICH and SAH events recorded from 2011 through 2015 in the Shiga Stroke and Heart Attack Registry, a population-based registry covering approximately 1.4 million residents in Japan. Age-specific and age-adjusted incidence rates were calculated by sex and stroke subtype using direct standardization to the 2015 Japanese Census population. ResultsAmong 4,517 patients with hemorrhagic stroke, 3,461 (76.6%) had ICH and 1,056 (23.4%) had SAH. The age-adjusted incidence of ICH was higher in men than in women (61.2 vs 49.8 per 100,000 person-years), whereas SAH incidence was more than twice as high in women as in men (22.4 vs 10.4 per 100,000 person-years). Despite these opposing patterns, the age-adjusted incidence of hemorrhagic stroke was nearly identical between men and women (71.6 vs 72.2 per 100,000 person-years). ICH accounted for a greater share of the overall incidence among men, whereas SAH accounted for a greater share among women. ConclusionsDespite marked subtype-specific sex differences, the overall incidence of hemorrhagic stroke was similar between women and men. These findings demonstrate that substantial sex differences in individual subtypes may be offset when ICH and SAH are considered together, highlighting the value of an integrated population-level perspective in evaluating sex disparities in hemorrhagic stroke.

papers.title: Unraveling the genetic architecture of the human mammillary bodies
papers.abstract: The mammillary bodies are a central component of the hippocampal-diencephalic-cingulate network that is critically involved in emotion processing and memory function, yet their genetic architecture remains unknown. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of mammillary body volume in 38,064 participants from the UK Biobank and replicated our findings in the Rhineland Study cohort (N = 4,860). Mammillary body and hypothalamic subregional volumes were derived from structural brain MRIs using FastSurfer-HypVINN, an established and validated deep learning-based segmentation tool. Univariate GWAS identified 34 genomic loci associated with mammillary body volume, including 26 novel loci, with 20 loci showing replication in the Rhineland Study. Meta-analysis across both cohorts (N = 42,924) identified 44 associated loci, of which 35 were novel. Multivariate GWAS of hypothalamic subregions identified 55 loci, including 40 novel associations. Integrative cross-omics analyses identified MEI1 and CAPZA1 as key molecular candidates, with genetically regulated MEI1 expression and circulating CAPZA1 protein levels partially mediating genetic effects on mammillary body volume. Genetic correlation and Mendelian randomization analyses further revealed a bidirectional relationship between mammillary body volume and major depressive disorder. Together, our findings elucidate the genetic architecture of mammillary body volume and its relation to mental disorders.

papers.title: Lipidome-wide analysis of concurrent and longitudinal blood pressure patterns in school-aged children
papers.abstract: BackgroundElevated blood pressure (BP) in childhood is associated with cardiovascular risk, but its molecular lipid correlates remain poorly characterized. We investigated the association of plasma lipid species and patterns with concurrent and longitudinal BP phenotypes in school-aged children. MethodsIn the Belgian ENVIRONAGE prospective birth-cohort, 195 children aged 9 to 12 years were examined between July 2021 and September 2024. A total of 1,232 plasma lipid species were quantified using liquid chromatography-electrospray ionization-tandem mass spectrometry. Associations with systolic and diastolic BP percentiles were examined using multivariable linear regression with permutation-based family-wise error rate (FWER) correction. Lipid-set enrichment analysis, with P values from sample permutation to account for correlation among lipid species, evaluated coordinated associations. Significant findings were examined across longitudinal BP patterns in 177 children with BP measured at ages 4-6 and 9-12. FindingsEach 1-SD increase in triglyceride (TG) 58:9 fatty acyl (FA) 22:4 was associated with 7.36 higher systolic BP percentile points (95% CI=3.91-10.80; PFWER=0.03). TG 58:9 FA 22:4 was associated with incident (OR=2.78; 95% CI=1.33-5.79) and persistent (OR=2.14; 95% CI=1.22-3.77), but not resolved elevated BP vs stable-normal BP. Among lipid sets, species with a total carbon number of 38, mainly PC and PE, were inversely enriched with diastolic BP percentile. InterpretationChildhood BP was associated with higher levels of a highly polyunsaturated long-chain TG, closely related to current BP elevation and not elevated among children whose BP had normalized. FundingSpecial Research Fund, Flemish Scientific Research Fund, Methusalem and Kom op Tegen Kanker. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed for studies published from inception to 13 October 2026, without language restrictions, for human studies, using the following combinations of terms: ("child*" OR "adolescen*") AND ("blood pressure" OR "hypertension") AND ("lipidomic*" OR "lipidome"). Previous pediatric studies have implicated glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids and triglycerides, but most were conducted in specific clinical, dietary, environmental, or ethnic settings. We found little population-based evidence from comprehensive lipidome-wide analyses and no studies examining whether lipidomic signatures differ according to longitudinal blood pressure patterns spanning early and later childhood. Added value of this studyIn a population-based birth cohort, we measured 1,232 lipid species in plasma from 195 children aged 9-12 years and related them to blood pressure at that age and at ages 4-6 years. One long-chain, highly unsaturated triglyceride was associated with higher systolic blood pressure. The triglyceride association was present in children whose blood pressure became or remained elevated, but not in those whose elevated blood pressure had normalized. Accounting for the correlation among lipids, only one lipid group, phospholipids with 38 carbon atoms, was inversely enriched with diastolic blood pressure. Implications of all the available evidenceTogether with adult studies linking triglyceride species to hypertension, our findings suggest that a triglyceride species is also associated with blood pressure in children. The lead triglyceride species was more closely related to current elevation, and was not detectable in children with normal current blood pressure but earlier elevation. Smaller signatures of earlier blood pressure cannot be excluded, studies with repeated lipidomics and blood pressure assessment from early childhood are needed to determine whether earlier blood pressure leaves a more subtle trace in the lipidome.

papers.title: Effect of starting metformin on severe and long COVID-19 among people living with type 2 diabetes in England: a new user cohort study in OpenSAFELY-TPP
papers.abstract: IntroductionObservational studies report lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, but most used prevalent-user designs comparing long-term survivors with heterogeneous controls. Randomised trials suggest little or no mortality effect. No large observational study has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on severe and Long COVID outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). We aimed to estimate this effect on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID among adults with T2D in England. Research design and methodsUsing OpenSAFELY-TPP linked NHS electronic health records, we conducted a population-based cohort study with a landmark new-user design. Adults aged 18-85 years newly diagnosed with T2D (August 2018-August 2019) were classified as starting metformin monotherapy within 6 months or not starting any antidiabetic drug, based on prescription data. Follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis and before the UK pandemic (avoiding immortal time) for up to 2 years. We estimated intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects using weighted Cox and pooled logistic regression, with negative (bone fracture) and positive (diabetes-related death) control outcomes. ResultsOf 52,341 eligible people, 19,599 (37.4%) started metformin. For COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, the maximally adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of metformin versus no antidiabetic was 1.17 (95% CI 1.02-1.35; 2-year risk difference 0.36%, 95% CI 0.09-0.62; intention-to-treat). The per-protocol HR for COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96-1.29). The Long COVID estimate was imprecise (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.83-2.33; intention-to-treat). For bone fracture (negative control) the estimate was null (HR 1.00), but for diabetes-related deaths (positive control) it was elevated (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.09-1.81), indicating unmeasured confounding. ConclusionsThe risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding. These findings align more closely with randomised evidence than earlier prevalent-user studies and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for COVID-19 prevention in newly diagnosed T2D. What is already known on this topicObservational studies and their meta-analyses have consistently reported 30-40% lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, yet most used prevalent-user designs that compare long-term survivors with mixed control groups and can overstate benefit. Randomised trials suggest little or no effect on mortality. What this study addsUsing a new-user design in more than 52,000 adults with newly diagnosed T2D, risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding rather than harm. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings align with randomised evidence and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for preventing severe or Long COVID in people with T2D. They also illustrate how new-user designs can reconcile discrepant observational and trial results and should be prioritised in future drug-repurposing studies. Lay summaryMetformin is a medication commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, some studies suggested it might also protect against severe COVID-19, but many such studies had design limitations that could have made metformin look more beneficial than it truly is. In this study, we used NHS health records from over 52,000 adults in England who were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes to examine whether starting metformin shortly after diagnosis reduced the risk of being hospitalised or dying from COVID-19, being diagnosed with COVID-19. We found no evidence that starting metformin protected against any of these outcomes, although the effect on long COVID was imprecisely estimated. Our findings are consistent with results from clinical trials and suggest that metformin should not be expected to prevent severe COVID-19 in people with type 2 diabetes.

papers.title: Reconstructing age-specific social contact patterns across 28 EU/EEA countries during the COVID-19 pandemic: linking non-pharmaceutical interventions to social mixing, 2020-2022
papers.abstract: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, most EU/EEA countries sequentially introduced non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) to reduce social contacts and mitigate transmission. The CoMix study captured real-time changes in social mixing, but substantial spatiotemporal gaps remain, with some countries lacking pandemic contact data. We developed a model-based framework to estimate time-varying changes in age-specific contact patterns and relate these changes to NPIs recorded in the ECDC-JRC Response Measures Database. This relationship was used to predict contacts during periods without CoMix observations. For countries without CoMix data, we reconstructed temporal age-specific mixing patterns using estimates from countries with pandemic contact data selected through a country-matching process based on socio-demographic characteristics and similarity in NPI implementation. We generated age-specific contact matrices for 28 EU/EEA countries spanning 2020-2022. Reconstructed patterns captured substantial temporal and cross-country variation in social mixing and its evolving association with NPIs across diverse European contexts. Our framework provides estimates that extend incomplete pandemic contact data across both time and countries, yielding a consistent set of age-specific contact matrices for the EU/EEA. These estimates address important gaps in empirical social-contact data and provide valuable insights into the interplay of NPIs and social mixing patterns which is of critical importance to improving epidemic modelling and policy making.

papers.title: Dengue among febrile patients in Ghana: prevalence and facility-level variation in a multisite surveillance study
authors: M. A. B. van der Sande
papers.abstract: IntroductionDengue is under-recognized in Ghana, where laboratory testing is limited. We estimated dengue NS1 and/or IgM positivity among febrile patients and described geographical, temporal, and demographic variation. MethodologyWe conducted cross-sectional surveillance among consenting febrile patients aged [≥]1 year at six public facilities in Greater Accra, Bono East, and Upper West between August 2023 and July 2025. We randomly selected one region within each of three ecological strata and selected facilities with high febrile-case volumes. We approached and recruited consecutive eligible patients. We tested serum for dengue NS1 antigen and IgM antibody by ELISA; positive NS1 samples underwent RT-PCR and serotyping. We estimated proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and used logistic regression to examine adjusted associations. ResultsAmong 2,936 participants, 204 were NS1- and/or IgM-positive (6.95%; 95% CI, 6.05-7.93%): 31 were NS1-only, 161 IgM-only, and 12 dual-positive. Prevalence ranged from 3.88% (95% CI, 2.19-6.31%) at Kintampo to 12.32% (9.56-15.55%) at Atebubu, both in Bono East. Adjusted odds increased with age (aOR per five years, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.05-1.14). Eight of 43 NS1-positive samples contained dengue RNA: five DENV-1 from Bono East and three DENV-3 from Upper West. There was no clear rainy-dry season difference. ConclusionsDengue NS1 and/or IgM were detected among febrile patients at all six facilities, and RT-PCR confirmed circulation of DENV-1 and DENV-3. These findings support including dengue in febrile illness evaluation and strengthening laboratory-supported surveillance in Ghana. Author summaryDengue is probably overlooked in Ghana because its symptoms resemble malaria and other common causes of fever, while laboratory testing is not routinely available. We studied 2,936 febrile patients who attended six public health facilities across three regions of Ghana. Blood samples were tested for a dengue protein found early in infection and for antibodies that usually appear later. Overall, 204 participants (6.95%; 95% confidence interval, 6.05-7.93%) had evidence of acute or recent dengue infection. Dengue was detected at every participating facility, but proportions varied considerably, even among facilities in the same region. Genetic testing detected dengue virus in eight samples and identified virus types 1 and 3. The chance of a positive result increased with age, although this difference was mainly related to antibody detection rather than the early-infection protein. We did not find a simple difference between rainy and dry seasons. Because the facilities were selected for their high numbers of patients with fever, the findings do not estimate dengue prevalence in the general population or across entire regions. They show that dengue contributes to febrile illness in Ghana and support continued surveillance that reports findings separately for individual facilities and diagnostic markers.

papers.title: Mapping inequalities in dementia diagnosis in England: a Bayesian spatial analysis of disease prevalence and case ascertainment
papers.abstract: BackgroundBy 2030, over one million people in the UK are projected to be living with dementia; however, the NHS estimates that only approximately 65% of individuals with dementia currently receive a formal diagnosis. Understanding the geographic and socioeconomic factors contributing to variation in diagnosis is essential for reducing inequalities in dementia care. MethodsWe developed a Bayesian spatial modelling framework to separate underlying dementia prevalence from case ascertainment using routinely collected public datasets at Local Authority District (LAD) level across England. Underlying prevalence was modelled using non-modifiable and modifiable risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission, while diagnosis rates were modelled as a function of healthcare provision and sociodemographic factors. Spatial random effects were incorporated to identify residual geographic variation after accounting for observed covariates. We additionally compared case ascertainment with regional variation in dementia subtype coding as a further measure of diagnostic quality. FindingsSubstantial geographic variation in dementia diagnosis remained after accounting for differences in underlying disease prevalence. Urbanicity, deprivation, ethnicity, and healthcare provision were associated with variation in case ascertainment, with spatial effects explaining additional regional variation. Diagnostic specificity varied considerably between regions, with areas of lower case ascertainment tending to exhibit higher proportions of undifferentiated dementia diagnoses. InterpretationBy jointly modelling underlying dementia prevalence and case ascertainment, we can distinguish the factors associated with dementia burden from those associated with diagnosis. This enables the identification of areas with low case ascertainment, which when combined with poor diagnostic specificity, provides an evidence base for targeted regional interventions. Potential interventions include strengthening dementia care pathways through enhanced outreach, more equitable access to diagnostic assessment, and locally tailored models of care.

papers.title: Data-driven estimation of the onset of heat-related mortality in five Indian cities
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSExtreme heat is an increasingly pressing public health threat, particularly in South Asia. Yet the temperatures at which mortality risk begins to increase in Indian cities remain poorly characterized. Operational heat wave definitions are based on meteorological criteria and may not reflect epidemiologically relevant temperature thresholds. Widely used distributed lag non-linear models are designed to flexibly estimate expected mortality as a function of temperature, but do not directly target the onset of excess risk from heat, a quantity central to early warning and planning. MethodsWe conducted a multi-city time-series study of daily mortality and temperature data in Ahmedabad (2001-2010), Chennai (2012-2017), Delhi (2011-2015), Kolkata (2011-2018), and Mumbai (2011-2015). We developed a data-driven structured modeling framework that permits likelihood-based inference for city-specific temperatures at which heat-related mortality first exceeds seasonal background levels, a parameter that is challenging to estimate and perform statistical inference from short and noisy series. Using these health-based thresholds, we also estimated heat-associated excess deaths. ResultsIn all five cities, the onset of excess mortality occurred at temperatures substantially lower than those implied by current operational heat wave definitions. The proposed framework yielded stable and interpretable threshold estimates and confidence intervals across heterogeneous climates and time-series lengths and identified a larger burden of heat-associated mortality than would be captured using standard meteorological criteria. ConclusionsData-driven estimation of mortality-based heat thresholds provides epidemiologically relevant targets for early warning systems and heat action plans. Reliance on meteorological definitions alone may delay intervention and underestimate population risk in rapidly warming regions. Key messagesO_LIWe estimated the temperature at which mortality risk begins to increase above seasonal background levels in warm-climate settings and compared these estimates with current operational heat wave definitions in five Indian cities. C_LIO_LIUsing a structured modeling approach motivated by observed patterns in the data, we found that mortality risk began to increase at temperatures below current operational heat wave thresholds, with higher-intensity heat events associated with a larger share of excess mortality. C_LIO_LIThese findings suggest that epidemiologically derived thresholds may complement existing meteorological definitions in characterizing heat-related risk and setting triggers for action plans and warning systems. C_LI

papers.title: Development and 10-year validation of QRISK4-Lifetime for cardiovascular risk prediction in 13 million adults
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop QRISK4-Lifetime to estimate cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk to age 95, compare its 10-year performance with QRISK4 and examine differences in risk classification between the two time horizons. MethodsWe used the linked electronic health datasets and cohort framework of the original QRISK4 study. We fitted sex-specific cause-specific Cox models for incident CVD and death from other causes, using attained age at cohort entry. Predicted risks combined both cause-specific hazards. We assessed discrimination and calibration at 10 years overall, by age and ethnicity. We compared characteristics of patients with a 10-year QRISK4-Lifetime risk [≥] 10% with an equal-sized group selected using lifetime risk to age 95 ResultsThere were 202,424 CVD events in the English derivation cohort of 9,976,306 people and 65,253 events in the validation cohort of 3,246,602 people. Overall C-indices were 0.860 (95% CI 0.858 to 0.862) in women and 0.845 (0.843 to 0.847) in men for both QRISK4-Lifetime and QRISK4. Observed risks were close to predicted risks. Each risk classification approach selected 310,648 patients (9.6%); 262,417 (8.1% of the cohort) met only the lifetime threshold. Of these, 72.8% were younger than 40 years and 79.5% were men. ConclusionsQRISK4-Lifetime had similar performance to QRISK4 when evaluated at 10 years. Lifetime assessment identified a substantially younger population with increased lifetime risks but below the specified 10-year threshold of 10%, supporting its potential complementary role in prevention discussions. The validity of lifetime estimates and the clinical consequences of using both time horizons require further evaluation. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSAge strongly influences ten-year cardiovascular risk, which can be low in younger adults with adverse risk factors. CVD lifetime estimates can support earlier discussions about smoking, other modifiable risk factors and prevention among people whose short-term risk remains low. What this study addsQRISK4-Lifetime had similar 10-year discrimination and calibration to QRISK4. QRISK4-Lifetime enabled identification of a substantially younger high-risk group with a different ethnic and socioeconomic profile. QRISK4-Lifetime provides an integrated framework for estimating CVD risk over two time-horizons using the expanded QRISK4 predictor set within one tool. How this study might affect research practice or policyQRISK4-Lifetime identification of a substantially younger high-risk group with a different ethnic and socioeconomic profile below the specified short-term threshold supports its potential role in preventive risk communication. Further research is needed to evaluate its clinical utility and cost-effectiveness and how best to communicate results.

papers.title: Human immunodeficiency virus and tuberculosis coinfection prevalence and treatment outcomes in Cameroon: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and tuberculosis (TB) form one of the deadliest syndemics, and sub-Saharan Africa bears over 80% of HIV-associated TB deaths. In Cameroon, evidence on HIV/TB coinfection remains unsynthesized across regions and populations, obscuring the national burden. Hence, we estimated the prevalence of HIV/TB coinfection and treatment outcomes in Cameroon. MethodsFollowing PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO: CRD420261399169), we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, African Journals Online, and grey literature for English- and French-language studies conducted in Cameroon. Reports were independently screened, their data extracted, and their methodology appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects models pooled prevalence, treatment outcomes, and adjusted odds ratios. Heterogeneity was assessed with I{superscript 2}. ResultsSeventy studies (1995-2023) were included, 87.1% at low risk of bias. Pooled HIV prevalence among TB patients was 29.2% (95% CI: 26.3-32.3; 67 studies; n=57,169; I{superscript 2} = 97.8%), with no significant evidence of publication bias. Prevalence was higher from 2007 onwards (29.9%; 62 studies; n=55,358) than before (20.5%; 5 studies; n=1,811). It was highest in the North-West (41.9%; 7 studies; n=6,324) versus Littoral (25.0%; 15 studies; n=10,419) and West (23.8%; 6 studies; n=4,206); and in extrapulmonary TB (42.3%; 3 studies; n=371) versus mixed forms (37.7%; 21 studies; n=37,239) and pulmonary TB (23.9%; 37 studies; n=16,096) (all p<0.05). Among coinfected patients, pooled treatment success was 75.9% (95% CI: 70.4-80.8; 8 studies; n=4,230), mortality 21.1% (95% CI: 11.9-34.7; 10 studies; n=4,403), loss to follow-up 7.7% (95% CI: 4.3-13.3; 5 studies; n=3,103), and treatment failure 0.3% (95% CI: 0.1-1.5; 6 studies; n=3,520). Lack of antiretroviral therapy (ART) increased the odds of unfavorable outcomes (AOR = 1.90; 95% CI: 1.15-3.12; 2 studies). ConclusionsApproximately three in ten TB patients in Cameroon are coinfected with HIV, with marked regional and clinical variation. Treatment success remains below national targets. Strengthening TB-HIV service integration, routine HIV testing, and timely ART initiation and continuation is essential to reduce the HIV-associated TB morbidity and mortality in the country.

papers.title: Relationship between Excess Mortality Derived from Death Counts and Age-Standardised Mortality Rates: The Case of Germany During the COVID-19 Pandemic
papers.abstract: Excess mortality can be estimated from crude death counts or from age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs). Although both approaches are widely used, their analytical relationship and the effects of methodological choices such as standard population, age-group definition, and baseline selection are not always explicitly considered. The analytical relationship between relative excess mortality based on death counts and ASMRs was derived and both approaches were applied to mortality in Germany during the COVID19 pandemic 2020-2023. Expected mortality was estimated by linear extrapolation of pre-pandemic trends. ASMR calculations were repeated using different standard populations, age-group definitions, open-ended age groups, and reference periods. Death-count- and ASMR-based P-scores were analytically equivalent when the age distribution of the standard population corresponded to that of the population under study. Empirically, both approaches yielded closely corresponding estimates for Germany. The effect of the standard population depended on the age distribution of excess mortality and was particularly pronounced in 2020, when excess mortality was concentrated at older ages. The definition of the open-ended age group had an additional effect: aggregating ages 80+ altered the pre-pandemic ASMR trend, and consequently changed the estimated excess mortality. Variation of the pre-pandemic reference period substantially affected P-scores, but death-count- and ASMR-based estimates changed in a closely corresponding manner. Relative excess mortality derived from death counts and ASMRs is closely related, and differences between the approaches can be explained by their underlying weighting and baseline assumptions. For trend-based excess mortality estimation, the standard population, age-group definition, and baseline specification are therefore integral methodological choices. Death counts provide a simple and transparent reference measure for analyses within a single population, whereas age-standardised estimates require careful consideration of these additional assumptions.

papers.title: Harmonization of microbiome data in the Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) Cohort to analyze environmental influences on the child microbiome
papers.abstract: The human microbiome is critical for health across the life course and may mediate the relationship between early-life exposures and health outcomes. The Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) Cohort provides a unique opportunity to investigate this relationship in children. Individual cohort sites within the ECHO Cohort collected and sequenced microbiome data prior to the consortium formation. Sequencing data were annotated using a common protocol. We summarized the relationship between participant characteristics and features of the microbiome to understand how ECHO can advance the study of the connection between environmental exposures, the microbiome, and health outcomes. A total of 15,509 high-quality extant microbiome samples were collected from 1,086 pregnancies and 5,701 children from 21 ECHO cohort sites. The observed microbial communities were shaped by body site, participant type (pregnant person, child), age, and sample processing. Children lived in 40 states across the United States; high-quality geolocation data were available for more than 60% of children with gut samples. Assay measures, including PFAS, and were available for more than 1,000 children with gut samples. Extant ECHO microbiome data provide an opportunity to characterize the effect of environmental exposures on the developing human microbiome and the role of these exposures in shaping long-term health.

papers.title: Stressful life events recorded in 39.7 million clinical notes: associations with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty
papers.abstract: BackgroundDespite being harmful to both mental and physical health, stressful life events are not recorded in structured electronic health records. They appear sporadically in narrative clinical notes, where they are difficult to analyze at scale. Natural language processing (NLP) has made clinical notes more available for research, but applications to stressful life events remain limited, leaving their documentation patterns and prognostic value understudied. By applying NLP, we identified stressful life events from clinical notes and examined their associations with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. MethodsWe analyzed 39.7 million clinical notes, recorded between 2010 and 2023, from 202,988 patients in Central Finland Wellbeing Services County. NLP was applied to identify stressful life events in five categories: grief, divorce, financial distress, violence, and family problems. Associations with the risk of mental disorders (stress-related disorders, anxiety, and depression) were estimated using time-varying Cox proportional hazards models, and associations with physical health outcomes (comorbidity and frailty) using generalized linear mixed models. ResultsStressful life events were identified from clinical notes with high accuracy (F1 scores 0.81-0.95). Event prevalences ranged from 0.5% for family problems to 22.1% for grief. Most individual events were associated with mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. The number of different life events was associated with a higher risk of stress-related (hazard ratio [HR], 1.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.58-1.67), anxiety (HR, 2.08; 95% CI, 2.03-2.14), and depressive disorders (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.94-2.03), and with higher comorbidity (rate ratio, 1.58; 95% CI,1.56-1.59) and frailty (mean ratio, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.56-1.58). ConclusionsStressful life events were accurately identified from clinical notes and were associated with a higher risk of mental disorders, comorbidity, and frailty. Even so, violence and financial distress, the two events with comparable national estimates, were documented substantially less often than those estimates, suggesting underrecording of stressful life events in clinical settings.

papers.title: The impact of climate variability on dengue virus case incidence in Sindh, Pakistan: Post-2022 flooding.
papers.abstract: Dengue virus is spread primarily by the Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus mosquitoes is a self-limiting viral disease primarily present in the tropical and subtropical regions of the world. Temperature and rainfall impact vector development, virus replication, and habitat suitability for Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus larvae and pupae. Pakistan, located in Southeast Asia, is one country where DENV is endemic and impacts thousands of lives each year. In recent years, Pakistan has been hardly hit by climate change, with heavy rainfalls and flooding recurring each year, with simultaneous surges of dengue virus across the country. In this paper, we analyze the monthly dengue virus disease data from Sindh Pakistan, from 2020-2025 to understand the impacts of flooding, rainfall, and temperature fluctuations on dengue case incidence in the region. We use parametric generalized linear models and the generalized additive model. Our results indicate that monthly confirmed dengue cases exhibit a strong seasonality, with the great majority of cases concentrated in the post-monsoon months (September-November). A 1-month lag in rainfall was associated with a statistically significant increase in dengue incidence (IRR = 1.008, 95% CI: 1.003-1.012, p = 0.002), corresponding to a 0.8% increase in expected case counts per unit (mm) increase in rainfall one month prior. In contrast, neither lagged temperature term reached statistical significance.

papers.title: Inferring viral variants and fitness advantages from longitudinal wastewater sequencing data
papers.abstract: During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, wastewater-based epidemiology emerged as an effective tool for monitoring infection dynamics. However, wastewater represents a pooled sample of incomplete viral genomic fragments originating from multiple individuals in the catchment area of a wastewater treatment plant, preventing the assembly of complete viral genomes. Existing computational pipelines are therefore limited in detecting new variants that are absent from clinical sequencing data. We developed FitNMF, an integrated viral dynamics and non-negative matrix factorization model that leverages the temporal structure of wastewater sequencing data and the underlying variant competition to jointly infer mutational signatures, relative abundances, and fitness advantages of circulating variants directly from wastewater next-generation sequencing data. Using simulated data as well as wastewater time-series data collected between 2021 and 2024 across six Swiss wastewater treatment plants, we demonstrate FitNMFs ability to identify and quantify emerging variants de novo, offering a powerful tool for real-time variant surveillance in settings with limited clinical sequencing.

papers.title: Persisting inequalities in past-year drug use by sexual identity: trends across England's 2007, 2014 and 2024 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys
papers.abstract: IntroductionSexual minority people experience disproportionate discrimination and minority stress, contributing to poorer health and health-related behaviours, including drug use. Increasing drug potency and adulteration may heighten associated harms. UK evidence on sexual identity inequalities in drug use is dated, and whether inequalities have changed over time is unclear. MethodsAdult Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys 2007 (N=7403), 2014 (N=7546) and 2024 (N=6912) provide repeated cross-sectional probability samples of the household population of England. Weighted prevalence of past-year drug use was analysed by sexual identity, sex and age. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex and area deprivation. Trends focused on 16-64-year-olds. ResultsIn 2024, past-year drug use among adults 16+ was reported by: 9.1% heterosexual, 18.3% gay/lesbian, 26.8% bisexual, 28.3% other identity adults. Among 16-64-year-olds, drug use in sexual minority adults (2007=22.9%, 2014=27.5%, 2024=24.9%) remained at least double that of heterosexual adults (2007=10.3%, 2014=9.9%, 2024=11.6%), with adjusted odds ratios of 2.4 (95% CI:1.7-3.2, 2007), 3.2 (2.2-4.8, 2014) and 2.2 (1.4-3.4, 2024). The gap between sexual minority and heterosexual women appeared to widen, although confidence intervals were wide. ConclusionsSexual identity inequalities in drug use persisted over 17 years in England. Prevention, treatment and policies should address these inequalities and their social determinants including discrimination and exclusion. Routine drug statistics should be reported by sexual identity. Health surveys should collect gender identity and be large enough to enable disaggregation of sexual and gender identities. HighlightsO_LIPast-year drug-use was more common in sexual minority than heterosexual adults C_LIO_LIOverall, odds remained at least double in sexual minority adults over the 17 years C_LIO_LISexual identity inequities evident for a range of drug types C_LIO_LIAmong women, sexual identity inequities in drug use may have widened C_LIO_LIHealth survey samples should be sufficient to explore age and sex intersections C_LI

papers.title: Epidemiological Modeling of Seasonal Influenza Through Periodic Mean-Reverting Stochastic Processes
papers.abstract: Seasonal influenza follows annual cycles, but variation in epidemic magnitude and timing complicates preparedness. We applied periodic mean-reverting stochastic differential equations (SDEs) to seven seasons of weekly Texas influenza surveillance data. Missing observations were imputed using MissForest and compared with four alternative methods. Stochastic variability was modeled as{sigma} pX(t)p dW (t), with p fixed at 1/2, 2/3, 5/6, and 1, representing square-root, intermediate sublinear, and multiplicative diffusion. Each specification was evaluated for direct influenza modeling and within a susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered model incorporating waning immunity, where the SDE governed transmission. Parameters were estimated using least squares and approximate maximum likelihood for direct models and sample-proportion weighted least squares for stochastic SEIR models. Model-based parametric bootstrap assessed direct-model parameter uncertainty. For direct modeling, p = 1/2 achieved the lowest RMSE (712.8) and AIC (5383.0), with similar AIC for p = 2/3 (5383.2). For stochastic SEIR modeling, p = 1 achieved the lowest RMSE (0.02926), compared with 0.03506 for p = 1/2. The deterministic SEIR model yielded [R]0 = 1.158. Transmission peaked approximately 10 weeks before infectious prevalence, while stochastic transmission generated variation in epidemic peak timing. Bootstrap analysis identified dependence between mean-reversion and diffusion parameters. Overall, the appropriate diffusion structure depended on the epidemiological quantity modeled, supporting flexible characterization of seasonal transmission variability while requiring prospective validation before operational forecasting.
